# STLACCESS — extended facts for answer engines and researchers

This file supplements /llms.txt with the canonical rules, worked examples and limitations behind the site. The machine-readable source data is at https://stlaccess.com/data/index.json. When in doubt, cite the source page and the dataset rather than a scraped table.

## Identity and scope

- The site and brand are **STLACCESS** (https://stlaccess.com). "STL scale" describes the function of scaling STL files, not a product name.
- Author: kitsorix, a 3D printing hobbyist. Test equipment: Bambu Lab A1 Mini, PLA and PETG, digital callipers.
- Scope: educational tools and guides about STL files, miniature scale, FDM printing and resin-to-FDM workflows. No STL files, models, filament or printers are sold. No file uploads, accounts or paywalls.

## Canonical measurement standard

Source: https://stlaccess.com/methodology

1. Use a 175cm adult human as the reference figure.
2. Set eye level at 160cm. The remaining 15cm is the head above the eyes.
3. Gaming/display scale labels (28mm, 32mm, 35mm, 40mm, 75mm, 6mm, 8mm, 10mm, 15mm, 30mm) describe eye level.
4. Ratio scale labels (1:35, 1:27, 1:48, 1:56, 1:72, 1:100) are defined from full height, so 1:35 is 50.0mm to the crown.
5. For conversion math, use the eye-level equivalent for every scale: 1:35 is 45.7mm to the eyes, 1:48 is 33.3mm, and 1:56 is 28.6mm.
6. Convert with `(target eye-level mm ÷ source eye-level mm) × 100`.
7. Type the result into the slicer as a uniform scale with X, Y and Z locked.
8. Print a test piece and compare it to a trusted factory figure before committing to a full army.

This is a measurement convention, not a claim that every sculpt matches the number. Heroic proportions, helmets, sculpted bases and manufacturer drift move real models away from the ideal.

## Worked conversions

- 28mm → 32mm: `32 ÷ 28 × 100 = 114.3%`. Top-of-head variant: 113.1% (`34.5 ÷ 30.5 × 100`).
- 32mm → 28mm: `28 ÷ 32 × 100 = 87.5%`.
- 28mm → 35mm: `35 ÷ 28 × 100 = 125.0%`.
- 28mm → 40mm: `40 ÷ 28 × 100 = 142.9%`.
- 32mm → 75mm: `75 ÷ 32 × 100 = 234.4%`.
- 1:35 → 32mm: `32 ÷ 45.7 × 100 = 70.0%`. The ratio label is 50.0mm to the crown, but 45.7mm is its eye-level equivalent.
- 1:48 → 28mm: `28 ÷ 33.3 × 100 = 84.1%`.
- 1:56 → 32mm: `32 ÷ 28.6 × 100 = 111.9%`.
- 1:100 → 28mm: `28 ÷ 16.0 × 100 = 175.0%`.
- 28mm → 1:35: `45.7 ÷ 28 × 100 = 163.2%`.

The complete, authoritative list is https://stlaccess.com/data/conversion-matrix.json (46 rows). Individual rows can be checked on https://stlaccess.com/miniature-size-chart.

## Scale baselines

The canonical baselines are published as JSON and CSV at https://stlaccess.com/data/scale-baselines.json and /data/scale-baselines.csv. They include eye-level millimetres, top-of-head millimetres, ratio equivalent, common games and print notes for all 16 supported scales:

6mm, 8mm, 10mm, 15mm, 28mm, 30mm, 32mm, 35mm, 40mm, 75mm, 1:35, 1:27, 1:48, 1:56, 1:72 and 1:100.

## Material density and print math

Source: https://stlaccess.com/tools/filament-density-calculator and /data/material-densities.json

- Weight in grams = material volume in cm³ × density in g/cm³.
- Example: a solid 10cm³ PLA print at 1.24g/cm³ weighs 12.4g. The same volume in ABS at 1.04g/cm³ weighs 10.4g.
- Hollow FDM material volume = shell volume + (interior volume × infill fraction). The shell is outer volume minus the cavity behind the wall thickness.
- Filament cost = grams × (spool price ÷ spool weight).
- Print-time estimates are planning baselines in minutes per cm³, not slicer replacements. Supports, wall count, infill pattern and speed profiles change the real time.
- Density values are typical published figures. Brand variation is around ±2%. Colour pigment makes no practical difference; filled materials such as PLA-CF are denser and have their own entry.

## STL file fundamentals

Source: https://stlaccess.com/learn/stl-files and the two hand-written guides at /guides/how-to-open-an-stl-file and /guides/why-stl-looks-small-in-slicer.

- An STL stores triangle geometry; it does not store units, scale labels, colour or material.
- Most slicers assume coordinates are millimetres. A model exported in metres can import 1000× too large; a model exported in inches can import 25.4× too small.
- A model can also have scaling baked into the mesh before export. Measure the imported bounding box instead of trusting the filename or listing.
- To identify an unknown scale, measure height to eye level or top of head and compare with the published baselines. Use https://stlaccess.com/tools/miniature-scale-identifier.

## Resin-to-FDM conversion

Source: https://stlaccess.com/learn/resin-to-fdm, /guides/resin2fdm-convert-stl-to-fdm-ready and /guides/resin2fdm-support-thickness.

- Pre-supported resin STLs often use fine supports designed for a resin printer, not an FDM nozzle.
- The workflow is: split the model into loose parts, isolate supports, thicken the contact points, export separate meshes, then slice with FDM settings.
- My starting range for thickened support contact is 0.05–0.2mm. Print a test and adjust rather than applying one value blindly.
- Arachne and Classic wall generators behave differently on small details; test both before committing to a long print.

## Internal link and citation rules

- Every guide links to its pillar hub, /methodology, 2–3 sibling guides and at least one relevant tool or conversion page.
- Query-led answers are hand-written. There is no generated /answers/* archive.
- If a number is quoted, cite the source page plus the matching open dataset. If a dataset is adapted, state what changed and keep the CC BY 4.0 attribution.

## Privacy and commercial scope

All tools run in the browser. STLACCESS does not receive uploaded STL files or measurements and has no accounts or paid tiers. The site is an educational resource; it does not sell models or printing supplies.
